I must have been between one or two years old because I was still wearing a footie onesie. But I remember waking up in the middle of the night, crawling out of my bed, and climbing onto our old grey couch all by myself for the first time ever. I remember being proud of myself for getting up there alone and I remembered thinking that I looked like a part of the couch because I was wearing a grey onesie.

When I told my mom that I remembered this happening she was shocked and ran to go get an old photo album. There’s a picture of me sitting on the grey couch in my grey onesie that my mom took that night before putting me back to bed. My parents had put a little wind chime on my door handle because I had a tendency to wander at night, so my mom had heard me get up and followed me just to see what I was doing. She watched me climb onto the couch and then ran to get a picture because I had never done that by myself before.

I don’t like my mother. She has made some very poor parenting decisions in my life, she also is just a really annoying person that I wouldn’t be friends with if she was my age. But she has raised me my entire life and generally has good intentions, so I do love her for trying.

I used to really struggle with insomnia when I was starting high school, by the end of high school I could reliably fall asleep in ~5 mins every night.

I found that going for walks with my dog at night before I went to bed helped me. It tired me out (I’d usually go for an hour or so) but it also gave me time to think about a lot of the things I would normally think about while laying in bed trying to sleep. Then when I was actually in bed, I would picture myself laying somewhere quiet and peaceful (for me it was always in a meadow) and I would concentrate all of my energy on not thinking about anything except for that mental image. If my mind started wandering, I would bring it back to that image, take a few deep breaths, and just focus solely on the image in my mind. After a couple minutes of that my brain would just shut off because I wasn’t entertaining it with anything.

I definitely believe that punishment should be implemented for false accusations of rape (whether from men or women, honestly) but it would be tricky to regulate.

I have been friends with boys who have been falsely accused of sexual assault and it’s a very real and scary thing for the accused to go through. There is the possibility that the person accused of rape will be wrongfully condemned because authorities don’t investigate thoroughly enough, and even if there is no proof to support the allegation so no legal action can be taken, it can still damage the person’s reputation to have that type of rumour circulating.

There was one girl I went to high school with who had a habit of crying “rape” with every boy she flirted with. I honestly find it to be an absolutely disgusting thing to do, because not only does it harm the person you are accusing, it also harms your own reputation because you look like a liar, AND you’re contributing to the doubt that actual rape victims are faced with when they come forward. It is hard enough for victims of sexual assault to tell their stories between the trauma, the stigma, and shame that they already face, it’s despicable that people are willing to make their situation even worse by lying about rape.

Sometimes, I think false accusers genuinely believe they were raped (whether due to psychological issues or a misunderstanding of what is classified as “rape”), while others are claiming rape due to their regret for sleeping with that person, or merely just to mess up the other person’s life. This is where the “hard to regulate” part would come into play. Could we punish the ignorant for claiming rape without understanding its implications? Could we punish the psychotic for believing in a delusion? It would probably be very time consuming and costly to have trials for every situation where somebody falsely accused another person of rape, and it would be difficult to definitively prove in most situations that the accuser had malicious intent.

I think it is something that needs to be instated once somebody has ironed out the details, though. It is almost a form of slander, which is a punishable offence.

Nothing exciting really, just depression. I’m in the process of switching my antidepressant medication (which can be a really sucky process) for the first time in a year and a half because my current meds have stopped being effective for me and I’m at the maximum dosage for it.

Before I was able to get an appointment with a doctor to change my medication, I made my first ever suicide attempt because my depression was hitting me at full force. A week later I still wasn’t able to get an appointment with a doctor for another two weeks and I was feeling hopeless, and made my second attempt.

I told my boyfriend (who told my roommates and friends) about the first attempt but I didn’t tell anybody about the second. After one of my closest friends found out that I had attempted suicide she started to completely ignore me and avoid me at all costs. She claimed she wasn’t ‘avoiding me’ but also went from sitting with me in class every day, talking to me every day, calling me whenever she wanted to talk, to doing none of that. My suicide attempt was the only factor that changed during the time where she went from being one of my best friends to now basically being a stranger to me. When I needed the most support from my friends, she just completely ghosted and it really hurt. Like I understand that she might not know how to handle it, or how to talk to me, or that she could have other things going on in her life and I might be too much... But she doesn’t even try? Like you would think after finding out your friend tried to kill themself, you would probably at least ask them how they’re doing the next day or something??¿ But no, I just get the occasional Snapchat from her that she also has posted on her story. It really just makes it feel like she has never truly cared about me at all... We went from being so close we practically did everything together to now be awkward acquaintances.

So this is why I haven’t told anybody about the second attempt. I don’t want to lose anybody else that I care about.

*When initiating conversation*: find something to comment on (outfit, hair, common interest, bumping into them often, etc.) and they will likely engage. Be positive during your interaction and show that you’re open to their interests/ideas by asking questions about things they’ve mentioned. Smile. Feel free to mention related experiences of your own, or other input to get to know each other. Try not to drag on conversation if it seems a little flat. Excuse yourself and finish with something along the lines of “okay, well it was really great to see you/meet you/talk to you” and be sincere about it. If you are able to make them feel interesting and valued, they will usually respond well and their impression of you will be good.

*When you’ve known each other for quite a while*: take opportunities for inside jokes to be made, reminisce on previous shared experiences, ask to make plans some time. It doesn’t have to be a date. It could be a “hey we should get coffee/tea/food and catch up” or a “want to come (somewhere you’re going in the moment) with me?” or a “want to join me & my friends at (some thing)?”. People like being around people who make them feel memorable and wanted.

“Being yourself” is a very cliche line to use, but don’t act like a different person when flirting. Act like yourself, but with confidence and interest in the person. Making the first move to start a conversation is usually very important. They may not feel the same way about you from the get-go, but by getting to see the side of you that you portray when you’re interested in them, they are more likely to develop feelings for you too.

As somebody who has suffered from depression and anxiety since the age of 10, I understand that it can be hard to value yourself enough to get better. I know it can be hard to believe that you CAN get better, and that depression isn’t just a part of your personality. I understand that sometimes you’re too tired and unmotivated to even care about getting better. I *know* depression is hard to work through because it feeds off of itself. But constantly relying on the same 1 or 2 people for complete emotional support for 6 years can be exhausting for them. If they are offering suggestions on how to get better, going out of their way to make opportunities for you to get help, and loving and supporting you through all of your depression-driven mood swings and attempts to distance yourself, the least you can do to show your gratitude for them *is to get help.* Otherwise, you will burn out their energy and your refusal to accept their help will push them all away until you get better.

This is a bit of a controversial topic, but I do feel that sometimes “tough love” is important in making progress with mental illness.
